_about: Troubleshooting for common trouble codes. Keys are a code or a range (P0301-P0312). sev: 1 = safe to drive, fix when convenient; 2 = fix soon, can cause other damage or poor running; 3 = stop or drive gently to a shop. notes: tips for a maker group (names match makes.json groups). Gathered from common repair knowledge; always confirm with testing before buying parts.

P0010-P0025.what: The engine computer can't make the variable cam timing go where it commands, or the cam actuator's solenoid circuit has a fault.
causes: Low or dirty engine oil, or the wrong oil grade (cam phasers are moved by oil pressure)
Sticking or failed cam timing (VVT/oil control) solenoid
Worn or stretched timing chain or worn cam phaser
Wiring or connector fault at the solenoid (for the 'circuit' codes)
checks: Check the oil level and condition first; change it with the specified grade if it's old
Unplug the cam solenoid and check its resistance (usually about 6-13 ohms) and the connector for oil or corrosion
Listen for rattle at cold start (timing chain/phaser)
If the code returns after an oil change and a known-good solenoid, check timing chain stretch (cam/crank correlation)

notes.Ford: 3.5 EcoBoost (2011-2017 F-150/Expedition) and 5.4 3V V8: cam phaser and timing chain wear are well known, often with a cold-start rattle. 4.6 3V Mustang: check oil level and VCT solenoids first.
notes.GM: 3.6 V6 (2008-2017): P0008/P0017/P0011 together usually mean timing chain stretch, often from long oil change intervals.
notes.Toyota: VVT-i oil control valve screens clog on engines with sludge; clean or replace the OCV and change the oil.
notes.Hyundai-Kia: CVVT oil control valves are a common fix for P0011/P0014.
notes.VW: 2.0 TSI (EA888 gen 1/2): a failing timing chain tensioner can set cam correlation codes. Have it checked urgently: a jumped chain wrecks the engine.
notes.BMW: VANOS solenoids and low oil level are the usual causes. Clean or swap the intake and exhaust solenoids to see if the code moves.
notes.Honda: P0011/P1009 on K-series: VTC actuator or oil control solenoid, often with a cold-start rattle.

P0016-P0019.what: The crankshaft and camshaft sensors disagree about where the engine is: the valve timing is off from where it should be.
causes: Stretched timing chain or worn guides/tensioner
Cam phaser stuck out of position
Low oil pressure or dirty oil
Failing cam or crank sensor, or a damaged tone ring
Timing jumped a tooth after belt/chain work
checks: Check oil level and condition
Check cam/crank correlation values in live data or with a dealer tool if available
Inspect the cam and crank sensors and wiring
If the engine rattles at start-up, have the timing chain inspected before it fails

notes.Ford: 3.5 EcoBoost and 5.4 3V: timing chain stretch and cam phasers are a common cause.
notes.GM: 3.6 V6: timing chain stretch (often with P0008/P0009).
notes.VW: 2.0 TSI: timing chain tensioner. Don't keep driving it long.

P0030-P0064.what: The heater inside an oxygen sensor (which warms it up quickly) has an electrical fault.
causes: Failed heater inside the O2 sensor (most common)
Damaged wiring, often melted on the exhaust
checks: Check the O2 heater fuse
Unplug the sensor and measure the heater resistance across the two same-colored wires (usually 2-15 ohms; open = bad sensor)
Check for 12 V on the heater feed with the key on
Inspect the harness along the exhaust

P0068.what: The air the engine measures (MAF/MAP) doesn't match how far the throttle is open.
causes: Vacuum or intake leak after the throttle
checks: Look for cracked intake boots and vacuum hoses
Clean the MAF with MAF cleaner and the throttle body
Compare MAF g/s at idle with the expected value (roughly the engine size in liters x 0.8-1.0 g/s, warm)

notes.Ford: Common on Ford electronic throttle trucks; cleaning the throttle body and MAF and checking intake leaks fixes many.

P0087.what: Fuel pressure is lower than the engine computer wants.
causes: On direct injection engines: worn high-pressure pump or its cam follower
checks: Compare desired vs. actual fuel pressure in live data
Test fuel pressure with a gauge
Check pump power and ground
Don't run the tank nearly empty

notes.VW: 2.0 FSI/TSI: the high-pressure pump cam follower wears through. Inspect it; a worn-through follower damages the camshaft.
notes.BMW: N54/N55: high-pressure fuel pump failures are well known.
notes.Ford: EcoBoost: check low-pressure pump and the fuel pump driver module.

P0101.what: The mass air flow (MAF) sensor reading doesn't make sense for how the engine is running.
causes: Dirty MAF sensor (oiled air filters are a common cause)
Intake air leak between the MAF and the engine
checks: Inspect the air filter and intake duct for cracks or loose clamps
Clean the MAF with MAF-safe cleaner only (don't touch the wires)
Check MAF g/s at idle and at 2500 RPM against normal values
Check fuel trims: high positive trims together with this code point to an air leak or a dirty MAF

notes.Ford: Dirty MAF is very common on Fords; clean it first.
notes.Toyota: Clean the MAF; Toyota MAFs are sensitive to oil from oiled filters.
notes.GM: Check for a cracked intake duct and clean the MAF.

P0102-P0103.what: The MAF sensor signal is out of range electrically (too low or too high).
causes: Broken wire or short in the MAF circuit
Air leak or blocked air filter (low)
checks: Check the connector and wiring
Check MAF power (12 V or 5 V) and ground
Watch MAF reading in live data while wiggling the harness

P0106-P0109.what: The manifold pressure (MAP) sensor reading is wrong or out of range.
causes: Cracked or disconnected vacuum hose to the MAP sensor
Vacuum leak or mechanical engine problem (low vacuum)
checks: With key on, engine off, MAP should equal barometric pressure (about 100 kPa at sea level)
At warm idle MAP is usually about 25-40 kPa
Inspect the vacuum hose and connector

P0110-P0114.what: The intake air temperature sensor reading is wrong or out of range.
causes: Failed sensor (often built into the MAF)
checks: After the car sits overnight, intake air temp should match outside temperature and coolant temp
Check the connector and wiring

P0115-P0119.what: The engine coolant temperature sensor reading is wrong or out of range.
causes: Low coolant (sensor in an air pocket)
checks: Check coolant level
Cold engine: coolant temp should be close to outside temperature
Warm engine: should read about 85-105 °C (185-220 °F)
A reading of -40 means open circuit; a very high reading means a short

notes.Ford: Many Fords use a cylinder head temperature (CHT) sensor instead; see P1285-P1299 too.

P0120-P0124.what: The throttle or accelerator pedal position sensor signal is wrong or out of range.
causes: Worn or failed throttle position sensor
5 V reference problem shared with other sensors
checks: Watch throttle position in live data while slowly pressing the pedal: it should rise smoothly without jumps
Check the connector
If several sensor codes appear together, check the 5 V reference (P0641/P0651)

P0125.what: The engine takes too long to warm up enough for closed-loop fuel control.
checks: Watch coolant temperature: a healthy engine reaches about 80 °C (176 °F) within 10-15 minutes of driving
Check coolant level

P0128.what: The engine doesn't warm up to normal temperature in time. Almost always the thermostat is stuck open.
causes: Cooling fan running all the time
checks: Watch coolant temperature on a drive: it should reach about 85-105 °C (185-220 °F) and stay there
Poor cabin heat in winter is another hint
Check the fan isn't running constantly on a cold engine

notes.Chrysler: Common on the 3.6 Pentastar and older Jeeps (also see P1281).
notes.BMW: Electric thermostats (often with P0597) fail commonly.
notes.Subaru: Common; replace the thermostat with an OEM part.
notes.Ford: Common on 4.6/5.4 V8s.

P0130-P0167.what: An oxygen sensor's signal is out of range, slow, or not changing. Sensor 1 is before the catalytic converter, sensor 2 after it.
causes: Wiring damaged by exhaust heat, or a corroded connector
Engine actually running lean or rich (check fuel trims)
checks: Watch the sensor in live data at a steady 2000-2500 RPM, warm: upstream sensors should switch quickly between about 0.1 and 0.9 V; downstream sensors should be steadier, around 0.5-0.8 V
A sensor stuck near 0 V or 0.45 V usually has failed or has an open circuit
Check for exhaust leaks and wiring damage
Check fuel trims before replacing the sensor

P0171.what: The engine is getting too much air or too little fuel on bank 1, and the computer has added as much fuel as it's allowed to.
causes: Vacuum leak (cracked hose, PCV hose, intake gasket)
Weak fuel pump or clogged fuel filter
Exhaust leak before the upstream O2 sensor
checks: Look at long-term fuel trim: over +10% means the computer is adding fuel
If trims are high at idle but normal at 2500 RPM, look for a vacuum leak; if high everywhere, suspect fuel delivery or the MAF
Listen for hissing, check PCV and intake hoses; a smoke test finds hidden leaks
Clean the MAF sensor
Check fuel pressure

notes.Ford: Common: cracked PCV hose, intake manifold gasket, dirty MAF. If P0174 is also set, the cause is common to both banks (MAF, fuel pressure, a big vacuum leak).
notes.GM: LS V8s: intake manifold gaskets and the PCV system; 3.8 V6: lower intake gaskets.
notes.Toyota: Dirty MAF and cracked intake boot are the usual causes.
notes.VW: 2.0 TSI: failed PCV valve / oil separator diaphragm on the valve cover.
notes.BMW: Crankcase vent (CCV) valve, intake boot, DISA valve, and vacuum lines. Very common.
notes.Honda: PCV valve and hose, and intake gaskets.
notes.Subaru: Check for intake leaks and the PCV hose; on older EJ25s rule out head gasket issues.

P0174.what: Same as P0171 but on bank 2. If both are set, look for a cause common to both banks (MAF, fuel pressure, a large vacuum leak).

P0172.what: The engine is getting too much fuel or too little air on bank 1.
causes: Dirty or failing MAF reading too high
Coolant temperature sensor reading too cold
checks: Long-term fuel trim below -10% confirms it
Check the coolant temperature reading on a warm engine
Check fuel pressure and look for a leaking injector or regulator (fuel in the vacuum hose)
Check the purge valve isn't stuck open

P0175.what: Same as P0172 but on bank 2.

checks: Stop and let the engine cool. Don't open a hot radiator cap
Check coolant level and look for leaks
Check that the cooling fans run when hot or with the A/C on

causes: Towing or heavy load in hot weather
checks: Let it cool down
Check fluid level and condition
Watch transmission temperature: above about 120 °C (250 °F) is too hot

P0234.what: The turbo or supercharger is making more boost than it should.
causes: Vacuum/pressure line to the wastegate actuator off or cracked
checks: Ease off: overboost can damage the engine
Inspect wastegate lines and the actuator
Compare desired vs. actual boost

P0299.what: The turbo or supercharger isn't making as much boost as commanded.
causes: Boost leak (loose intercooler hose or clamp, cracked charge pipe)
Wastegate stuck open or a sticking actuator
Faulty boost control or bypass/diverter valve
checks: Inspect all intercooler hoses and clamps
Compare desired vs. actual boost in live data
Pressure-test the intake (boost leak test)
Check the wastegate actuator moves freely

notes.Ford: EcoBoost: intercooler condensation (stumble in humid weather), cracked charge pipe couplers, and wastegate rattle.
notes.VW: 2.0 TSI: torn diverter valve diaphragm or a split boost hose.
notes.BMW: N54: wastegate rattle and boost leaks at the charge pipe.

P0300.what: The engine is misfiring on more than one cylinder (or randomly). If the check-engine light is flashing, the misfire is bad enough to damage the catalytic converter.
causes: Worn spark plugs or failed coils/plug wires
Low fuel pressure or dirty injectors
Low compression, sticking valves or failing lifters
Crank sensor or tone ring problems (false misfires)
checks: If the light is flashing, reduce load and avoid hard acceleration
Use the app's misfire counts (menu) to see which cylinders are misfiring
Check fuel trims for a lean condition
Inspect spark plugs and coils
Do a compression test if misfires stay on one bank

notes.GM: 5.3/6.2 V8 with AFM/DFM: collapsed lifters cause misfires (often with ticking). P3400 alongside points there.
notes.Chrysler: HEMI with MDS: lifter/cam wear. 2011-2013 3.6 Pentastar: left cylinder head valve seat problems (misfires on cylinders 2/4/6).
notes.Honda: V6 with VCM: fouled plugs and stuck piston rings from cylinder deactivation are common.
notes.Subaru: EJ25: coils, and head gasket leaks on older engines.
notes.VW: Direct injection: coil packs and carbon buildup on intake valves.
notes.Ford: 4.6/5.4 3V: coil boots and plugs (3V plugs can break on removal; use the Ford procedure).

P0301-P0312.what: One specific cylinder is misfiring (the last digit is the cylinder number). A flashing check-engine light means stop driving hard.
causes: Bad spark plug or ignition coil on that cylinder (most common)
checks: Swap that cylinder's coil with a neighbor's, clear codes and drive: if the misfire moves, replace the coil
Inspect and replace the spark plug (check the gap and for oil or cracks)
Swap the injector or listen to it with a screwdriver/stethoscope
Compression test that cylinder

notes.Ford: Ford V8 cylinder numbering: 1-4 on the passenger side (front to back), 5-8 on the driver side.
notes.GM: GM V8: odd cylinders (1,3,5,7) on the driver side, even on the passenger side.
notes.Chrysler: Chrysler V8: odd on the driver side, even on the passenger side.

P0325-P0334.what: A knock sensor circuit has a fault, so the engine computer may pull timing and the engine can feel sluggish.
causes: Damaged wiring (often under the intake manifold)
checks: Check the connector and wiring
Measure sensor resistance against spec
Make sure it's torqued to spec

P0335-P0339.what: The crankshaft position sensor signal is missing or erratic. The engine may stall or not start.
checks: Watch RPM while cranking: 0 RPM while cranking points to the crank sensor
Inspect the sensor and connector
Check the 5 V supply and ground

notes.Nissan: VQ and QR engines: crank and cam sensors are a well-known failure (stalling, no-start).

P0340-P0349.what: A camshaft position sensor signal is missing or erratic.
checks: Inspect the sensor and connector for oil
Check the 5 V supply and ground
Check battery voltage while cranking (should stay above 9.6 V)

notes.Ford: 5.4 3V: cam sensors and connectors soaked with oil.
notes.Nissan: Cam sensors commonly fail on Nissans (stalling, hard start).

P0351-P0362.what: The ignition coil for one cylinder has a circuit fault, usually causing a misfire on that cylinder.
checks: Swap the coil with another cylinder and see if the code follows
Check the connector for 12 V feed
Check for a misfire code on the same cylinder

P0401.what: The engine computer sees too little exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) flow.
causes: Failed EGR pressure (DPFE) sensor or cracked hoses
Vacuum supply problem to a vacuum EGR valve
checks: Inspect EGR hoses and vacuum lines
Command the EGR open with a scan tool (the idle should stumble)
Clean carbon from the EGR valve and passages

notes.Ford: Pre-2008 Fords: the DPFE sensor and its rubber hoses are the classic cause. Replace the hoses and check the DPFE sensor first.
notes.Honda: Clogged EGR ports in the intake manifold are common (P1491 too).
notes.Nissan: EGR volume control valve and carbon.

P0420.what: The catalytic converter on bank 1 isn't cleaning the exhaust as well as it should. The downstream oxygen sensor is switching almost as much as the upstream one.
causes: Exhaust leak near the downstream O2 sensor
Engine misfire or rich running that damaged the converter
Oil or coolant burning in the engine
checks: Fix any misfire, fuel trim or O2 sensor codes first
Watch the downstream O2 sensor warm at 2500 RPM: a good converter gives a fairly steady 0.5-0.8 V; a switching signal means the converter is weak
Check for exhaust leaks before and around the downstream sensor
Aftermarket converters often trigger this again; use a CARB/OEM-grade one

notes.Toyota: Very common on high-mileage Toyotas; check the A/F sensor and for oil burning before replacing the converter.
notes.Subaru: Very common; check the front A/F sensor and use an OEM converter.
notes.Honda: Common; confirm with the downstream O2 sensor.
notes.Ford: Check the downstream O2 sensors; on Mustangs, aftermarket X/H-pipes without converters set this.

P0430.what: Same as P0420 but on bank 2.

P0440-P0441.what: A fault in the fuel vapor (EVAP) system: the purge flow or the system as a whole isn't working right. No effect on how the car drives.
causes: Purge valve stuck or not opening
Failed charcoal canister or vent valve
checks: Check the gas cap
Inspect EVAP hoses at the canister and engine
Command the purge valve with a scan tool and listen for clicking

P0442.what: A small fuel vapor leak (about 1 mm / 0.040 in) was found in the EVAP system. It doesn't affect driving.
causes: Loose, worn or wrong gas cap (most common)
Cracked EVAP hose or loose connection
Leaking filler neck or charcoal canister
checks: Tighten or replace the gas cap (check the seal)
Inspect EVAP hoses near the tank and canister
A smoke test finds small leaks quickly
After fixing, the monitor can take several days of driving to run again

notes.Honda: Honda also uses P1456/P1457 for the same kind of leak.
notes.Ford: Capless fillers: clean the filler neck flaps.

P0446.what: The EVAP canister vent valve (which seals the system for leak testing) isn't working right.
causes: Clogged vent valve or filter (mud, spider webs)
checks: Locate the vent valve near the canister or tank and check for dirt
Command it closed with a scan tool and listen
Check the connector

notes.GM: Vent solenoids near the tank on trucks clog and fail often (also P0449/P0455).
notes.Toyota: Canister and vent valve are a common cause.

P0455.what: A large fuel vapor leak (or no seal at all) in the EVAP system.
causes: Gas cap missing or not tightened
checks: Check the gas cap first
Look for disconnected hoses at the canister and purge valve
Smoke test

notes.GM: Vent solenoid near the tank and purge solenoid on the engine are common.
notes.Ford: 2011+ Ford: canister purge valve sticking open is common (hard start right after fueling is a hint).

P0456.what: A very small fuel vapor leak (about 0.5 mm / 0.020 in) in the EVAP system. Usually the gas cap or a tiny hose crack; it doesn't affect driving.

P0457.what: The EVAP system detected that the fuel cap is loose or missing.
causes: Gas cap loose, missing or worn
Debris on the filler neck seal
checks: Tighten the cap until it clicks, or replace it
The code clears itself after several drive cycles once fixed

P0496.what: Fuel vapor is being drawn into the engine when it shouldn't be: the purge valve is stuck open.
checks: Unplug the purge valve hose at idle: there should be no vacuum when it isn't commanded
Hard starting right after refueling is a classic symptom

notes.GM: Very common on GM trucks and SUVs.

P0500-P0503.what: The vehicle speed sensor signal is missing or wrong. The speedometer, shifting and ABS may act up.
causes: Wheel speed sensor problem on cars that use ABS sensors for speed
checks: Does the speedometer work?
Inspect the sensor and connector
Check ABS codes too

P0505-P0507.what: The idle speed isn't what the engine computer wants.
causes: Dirty throttle body or idle air control valve
checks: Clean the throttle body
Check for vacuum leaks (high idle)
After cleaning, some cars need an idle relearn procedure

P0520-P0524.what: The engine oil pressure is low, or the oil pressure sensor reading is out of range.
causes: Worn oil pump or engine bearings
checks: Stop and check the oil level now
Check oil pressure with a mechanical gauge to tell a bad sensor from real low pressure
Don't drive if oil pressure is really low

notes.GM: 5.3/6.0 V8: the oil pressure sensor and its screen fail often.
notes.Chrysler: 3.6 Pentastar and HEMI: oil pressure sensor/switch failures are common.

P0562.what: The engine computer sees low system voltage.
causes: Loose or corroded battery cables or grounds
checks: Check battery voltage: about 12.6 V engine off, 13.8-14.7 V running
Clean and tighten battery terminals and engine grounds
Have the battery and alternator load-tested

notes.Chrysler: Some 2008-2015 models: the TIPM (power distribution module) can cause electrical faults.

P0563.what: System voltage is too high, usually an overcharging alternator.
causes: Poor ground at the voltage sense
checks: Running voltage above about 15 V confirms it
Check grounds

P0597-P0599.what: The electrically heated thermostat circuit has a fault.
checks: Measure the heater resistance at the thermostat connector
Check for P0128

notes.BMW: Very common; the thermostat is usually replaced as a unit.

P0600-P0610.what: The engine computer found an internal problem.
checks: Check battery and charging voltage and grounds first
Check for software updates (dealer reflash)
Only replace the computer after power and grounds test good

notes.Ford: P0606 on Fords often comes with electronic throttle problems; check for TSBs and reflash.

P0641-P0653.what: A 5 V reference circuit that feeds several sensors is shorted or open, which often sets codes for many sensors at once.
causes: A shorted sensor pulling the reference down
checks: Unplug sensors on that reference one at a time; when the voltage comes back to 5 V, the last one unplugged is shorted

P0700.what: The transmission computer has stored its own trouble code and asked the engine computer to light the check-engine light. This code only says 'look in the transmission computer'.
checks: Read the codes from the transmission computer (TCM)
Check the transmission fluid level and condition

P0705-P0709.what: The transmission range sensor (gear selector position) signal is wrong.
checks: Watch the selected gear in live data while moving the shifter
Inspect the connector at the transmission

P0710-P0714.what: The transmission fluid temperature sensor reading is wrong or out of range.
causes: Failed sensor (often part of the internal harness)
checks: Compare transmission temp with coolant temp after a drive
Check the connector at the transmission

P0715-P0723.what: A transmission speed sensor (input/turbine or output) signal is missing or erratic. Shifting may be harsh or erratic.
causes: Metal debris on a magnetic sensor
checks: Inspect the connector
Check the sensor resistance and for metal debris

P0729-P0736.what: The transmission's actual gear ratio doesn't match the gear it commanded, meaning something is slipping.
causes: Faulty shift or pressure control solenoids
checks: Check fluid level and condition (burnt smell, dark color)
Note which gear slips
Check for solenoid codes

notes.Ford: 6R80 (F-150, Expedition): a fluid change and valve body/solenoid body issues are common causes. 5R55S (2005-2010 Mustang): servo/band wear.
notes.Honda: Honda/Acura 5-speed automatics of the early 2000s had known clutch pack failures.

P0740-P0744.what: The torque converter clutch (lockup) isn't working as commanded.
checks: Check fluid
Watch for RPM flaring at highway speed (TCC not locking)

P0745-P0799.what: A transmission shift or pressure control solenoid has a fault. Shifting may be harsh or stuck in one gear (limp mode).
checks: Check fluid level and condition
Check the transmission connector for fluid or corrosion
Measure the solenoid resistance through the connector

P0840-P0878.what: A transmission fluid pressure sensor/switch reading is wrong.
causes: Failed pressure switch (often part of the valve body)
checks: Check fluid level
Check the connector

notes.GM: 6-speed automatics: the pressure switch manifold is a common failure.

checks: Check fluid level now
Check fluid level and condition

P0A80.what: One or more blocks in the hybrid battery pack have weakened.
checks: Clean the hybrid battery cooling fan intake (usually near the rear seat)
A hybrid battery test can identify weak blocks

notes.Toyota: Very common on high-mileage Priuses and Camry hybrids.

P2096-P2099.what: The downstream O2 sensor shows the fuel mixture after the converter is too lean or rich, and the computer's fine-tuning has hit its limit.
checks: Check for exhaust leaks
Check upstream sensor response and fuel trims

notes.Mazda: Common on Mazda 3/6 with aging upstream sensors or exhaust leaks.

P2100-P2119.what: The electronic throttle isn't responding as commanded. The car may go into reduced power (limp) mode.
causes: Failed throttle motor or throttle body
checks: Clean the throttle body (key off)
Check the connector
Some cars need a throttle relearn after cleaning

notes.Ford: Ford ETC throttle bodies fail commonly (P2111/P2112/P2135); check for extended warranty/TSB coverage.

P2135-P2140.what: The two signals from the throttle (or pedal) position sensor don't agree. The car often goes into reduced power mode.
causes: Failed throttle body or pedal sensor
checks: Inspect the connectors at the throttle body and pedal
Watch both position signals in live data while pressing the pedal

P2177-P2194.what: The fuel mixture is too lean or rich at idle, off idle, or under load. Lean codes have the same causes as P0171, rich codes as P0172.

P2195-P2198.what: The upstream O2 (air-fuel) sensor reads stuck lean or rich.
checks: Check fuel trims
Check for exhaust leaks before the sensor
Watch sensor response

P2270-P2277.what: A downstream oxygen sensor (after the catalytic converter) has stayed lean or rich for too long when the computer expected it to change. 'Lean' means its voltage is stuck low.
causes: Exhaust leak before or near the sensor letting in outside air (makes it read lean)
Damaged sensor wiring touching the exhaust
The engine actually running lean or rich on that bank (check for P0171/P0174 or P0172/P0175)
checks: Watch the sensor in live data, warm, at a steady 2000-2500 RPM: a healthy downstream sensor sits around 0.5-0.8 V. One stuck near 0.0-0.1 V is reading lean
Snap the throttle or briefly add propane/brake cleaner near the intake: a working sensor jumps up toward 0.8-0.9 V
Check for exhaust leaks at the manifold, flex pipe and pipe joints ahead of the sensor
Inspect the sensor's connector and wiring along the exhaust
Check long-term fuel trim on that bank

notes.Ford: Ford V8s: bank 1 is the passenger side, bank 2 the driver side. On 2005-2010 Mustang GTs, P2270/P2272 commonly come from aging downstream sensors or aftermarket exhaust (off-road X/H-pipes). If one O2 tile in the app reads a flat 0.00 V, that's probably the sensor this code is about.

P2279.what: An air leak in the intake was detected. Same causes and checks as P0171 (vacuum leak).

P2646-P2649.what: The variable valve lift system (rocker arm actuator) isn't working as commanded.
causes: Low oil level or dirty oil
Failed VTEC/rocker arm oil pressure switch
checks: Check oil level and change the oil
Check the oil pressure switch and solenoid screen

notes.Honda: K-series VTEC: the oil pressure switch and the solenoid gasket/screen are common fixes.

P3400-P3497.what: The cylinder deactivation (fuel saver) system has a fault.
causes: Low oil level or wrong oil
Failed deactivation solenoid (valve lifter oil manifold)
checks: Check oil level and use the specified oil
Listen for lifter tick
Check for misfire codes

notes.GM: 5.3/6.2 AFM/DFM: lifters and the valve lifter oil manifold (VLOM) are common failures.

U0001-U0029.what: A problem with the network (CAN bus) that the car's computers use to talk to each other.
causes: Damaged or corroded wiring/connectors on the network
Aftermarket accessories spliced into the network
checks: Check battery voltage and grounds
Measure resistance across OBD pins 6 and 14 with the battery disconnected (about 60 ohms is normal)
Unplug modules one at a time to find one pulling the bus down

U0073-U0074.what: A computer's network connection (communication bus) is turned off due to errors.

U0100-U0300.what: One computer stopped hearing messages from another computer (named in the title).
causes: The named module lost power or ground (check its fuses)
Weak battery or a voltage drop when cranking
checks: Check the named module's fuses, power and ground
Check battery voltage, especially while cranking
Clear codes and see if it returns; a single old U code after a battery change is often harmless

notes.Ford: U0100 with stalling on Fords: check the PCM connectors and grounds.
notes.Nissan: Nissan uses U1000/U1001 for the same kind of fault.

U0401-U0428.what: A computer received data from another module that is invalid or out of range.
causes: A fault in the sending module (check it for codes)
Mismatched software after a module replacement
checks: Read codes from the sending module
Check battery voltage
Check for software updates

C0035-C0050.what: A wheel speed sensor circuit has a fault. The ABS and traction control lights usually come on and those systems are turned off (normal brakes still work).
causes: Dirt or rust on the sensor or tone ring
checks: Inspect the sensor wiring at that wheel
Compare all four wheel speeds in a scan tool while driving slowly
Measure the sensor resistance if it's a passive sensor

P1000.what: Not a fault. The computer hasn't finished all its self-tests since the battery was disconnected or codes were cleared.
causes: Recent battery disconnect or code clear
checks: Drive normally for several days, including some highway driving; it clears by itself

P1131-P1152.what: Ford: the upstream O2 sensor didn't switch as expected; it's stuck lean or rich, or the fuel correction hit its limit. Lean versions usually have the same causes as P0171 (vacuum leak, MAF, fuel pressure).

P1260.what: The immobilizer didn't recognize the key, so the engine was disabled.
causes: Faulty transceiver ring around the ignition
checks: Try a spare key
Check battery voltage
A dealer or locksmith can program keys

P1285-P1299.what: Ford: the cylinder head is too hot (or its temperature sensor reads wrong). The engine may shut off cylinders to cool itself.
causes: Failed thermostat, fan or water pump
Failed CHT sensor (for the circuit codes)
checks: Stop and check the coolant when cool
Check the cooling fan works
Compare CHT with coolant temp

P1400-P1406.what: Ford: the EGR pressure feedback (DPFE) sensor or its hoses have a fault.

P1450.what: The EVAP system pulled too much vacuum: usually a blocked vent or a stuck purge valve.
checks: Inspect the vent valve near the tank for dirt or spider webs
Check the purge valve

P1456-P1457.what: Honda: EVAP leak, P1456 on the fuel tank side (start with the gas cap), P1457 on the canister side (often the canister vent shut valve).

P1281.what: Chrysler: the engine took too long to warm up; usually the thermostat is stuck open.

P1326.what: Hyundai/Kia's knock sensor system detected the vibration pattern of worn connecting rod bearings. The engine may limit power to protect itself.
causes: Connecting rod bearing wear (Theta II and some other engines)
checks: Contact a Hyundai/Kia dealer: many engines with this code are covered by a recall/extended warranty
Avoid hard driving until checked
Check oil level

P1491.what: Subaru: the crankcase ventilation (PCV) system has a leak or fault.
checks: Inspect the PCV hoses for cracks or disconnection

P1610-P1615.what: Nissan's immobilizer (NATS) doesn't recognize the key or computer.
checks: Try a spare key
A dealer or locksmith can register keys

P1870.what: GM 4L60-E/4L65-E: the transmission is slipping, very often from a worn valve body (TCC regulator valve bore).

P1101.what: Ford: the MAF sensor didn't pass its self-test. Same checks as P0101.
